problems.description: Replaced SQLite-native AUTOINCREMENT with manual id assignment (SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id),0)+1) — but INTEGER PRIMARY KEY already auto-increments in SQLite, so the manual scheme is both redundant and racy under concurrent creates (two requests can compute the same next_id, causing an integrity failure). This introduces a correctness risk the seed did not have.

test_ids_assigned_manually_incrementing asserts strict id contiguity (t2.id == t1.id + 1), codifying the fragile manual-id scheme as an invariant instead of asserting uniqueness/monotonicity, which is what the app actually needs.

Measured convention score 0.72 is repo-wide; all listed violations (PascalCase/UPPER_CASE) live in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, conftest.py, notifications.py). The commit's own lines (app.py, test_app.py) are convention-clean — flagging the discrepancy between the score and the diff.

strengths: Fixes a real bug: created tasks were INSERTed with status 'done' but returned to the client as 'pending'.
Adds input validation (non-string/blank/whitespace titles now correctly 400) beyond the original empty-string check.
Adds a thorough 113-line pytest suite covering create/list/get/update CRUD plus edge cases (missing body, blank title, 404s), with an isolated tmp_path DB fixture.

Reduces smells (-1, SonarQube): removes dead/legacy helpers (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task) and adds consistent type hints while preserving the existing get_db, route, and jsonify response patterns.
commit_reviews.summary: A strong greenfield session that fixes the status bug, hardens input validation, and ships a solid test suite while cutting dead code, but the manual MAX(id)+1 id scheme replaces SQLite's native AUTOINCREMENT with a concurrency-unsafe pattern — and the measured 0.72 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.

problems.description: Pre-existing tasks get owner_id = NULL and become invisible to every owner-scoped query (get_tasks/get_task filter on owner_id); the migration preserves the rows but leaves no backfill or admin path to ever reach them.

create_task still uses the deprecated datetime.utcnow() (naive UTC) while generate_token uses tz-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) — inconsistent datetime handling that will break naive-aware comparisons.
Hardcoded dev JWT_SECRET fallback and no minimum password length; acceptable for a story session but should require an env var and stronger password validation in production.

The mechanical convention score (0.72, 10 violations) is repo-wide, not commit-specific: the enumerated violations live mostly in files this commit does not touch (celery_config.py, conftest.py, notifications.py), and app.py's listed 'Classes should use PascalCase' is not introduced by this diff (no classes added).

strengths: Owner scoping enforced at the data layer (WHERE owner_id on every task query), so all existing routes inherit the isolation consistently rather than only the new ones.
Follows the established codebase pattern exactly: model-layer functions, route-layer functions, section-comment separators, and the get_db() context manager.
Idempotent, non-destructive migration via PRAGMA table_info with an explicit, documented decision for legacy rows.
Clean decorator-based auth using @wraps + g.current_user with a single consistent 401 JSON shape across missing/invalid/unknown-user tokens.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-fitted feature-addition commit that slots cleanly into the existing layered Flask patterns and correctly scopes tasks by owner — flagged discrepancy: the 0.72 mechanical convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files, not this commit, though it does leave pre-auth tasks unreachable and introduces a deprecated datetime API.

problems.description: Email fallback fabricates 'username@example.com' for legacy users and when email is omitted; harmless while delivery is a mock, but if a real provider is ever wired in these derived addresses would be sent mail. Documented in the migration docstring, but the derivation is embedded in both create_user and get_user_email.

celery_config.py module-level constants are lowercase (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes), violating the repo's UPPER_CASE rule; this is a necessary deviation because Celery's config_from_object reads attributes case-sensitively — flagging it here only because the mechanical linter counts it.
send_notification_email uses print() alongside logger.info, a redundant second output channel; likely intentional for story-harness observability but a small smell.
edit_task now performs a second DB read (get_task before update_task) to detect the status transition; negligible at this scale and buys correct trigger semantics.

strengths: Notification fires only on a genuine status transition to completed — guarded against recompletion, title-only edits, and non-completed statuses, each covered by a dedicated test
_migrate_add_email faithfully mirrors the existing _migrate_add_owner_id pattern (PRAGMA table_info guard + ALTER TABLE + commit), with a docstring that documents the legacy NULL-email behavior

Clean separation of Celery wiring into celery_config.py + notifications.py with idiomatic config_from_object usage; broker default targets Redis 6379, consistent with the story-agent convention in this harness
New public signatures carry type hints (email: str | None = None) and the register endpoint validates email before persisting, matching existing request-validation style
commit_reviews.summary: A well-tested, pattern-consistent integration of async email notifications via Celery that improves the app; the mechanical convention score of 0.72 over-penalizes it because the analyzer flags conftest.py (untouched by this diff) and Celery config attributes that must be lowercase for config_from_object, so qualitative convention adherence is slightly higher (~0.8).

problems.description: A full ABC-based repository layer (BaseRepository + per-entity repositories) may be over-engineered for an app of this size; a lighter data-access seam would achieve the same decoupling.

The pre-existing SELECT COALESCE(MAX(id),0)+1 id-generation scheme is carried forward into the repository unchanged; it remains a latent race condition under concurrency (moved, not newly introduced).
user_repository/task_repository are module-level singletons instantiated at import time; this works because get_db is injected lazily, but it couples repository construction to app import order.

The measured convention score (0.72) reflects violations in files largely outside this diff (celery_config.py, conftest.py, notifications.py); the commit's own additions use PascalCase classes and snake_case functions as expected.

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: all SQL moved out of route handlers into a dedicated repository layer, keeping Flask routes thin.
Test-aware design — injecting the get_db callable (not a connection) means per-test app.DATABASE reassignment keeps working.
No new SonarQube bugs, smells, cognitive complexity, or duplications introduced by the refactor.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, test-aware repository refactor that improves layering without new debt, though the 0.72 convention score is driven mostly by pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit (flagged discrepancy).

problems.description: list_page_for_owner runs COUNT(*) plus a limit+1 scan on every page; O(n) per request and not scalable, though acceptable at this app's scale.
rate_limit_key re-decodes the JWT on every request inside the limiter key function, coupling rate-limit keying to auth internals; a middleware-level user context would avoid repeated decode cost.

New hard runtime dependency on Redis for rate limiting (default redis://localhost:6379/2) and a new dedicated test Redis on port 6399 in conftest.py — both must be provisioned or the app/tests fail at startup/run.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination is idiomatic and correct: limit+1 has_more detection, id-DESC ordering with the id-monotonicity assumption documented in the docstring, and a clean data/next_cursor/total envelope.
Rate-limit keying is well designed — per-user by JWT subject with IP fallback for unauthenticated routes (login/register).
Test isolation is handled properly: conftest.py points rate limiting at a dedicated Redis (6399) and flushes per test so counts never bleed across tests.
Comprehensive, consistent test coverage: existing tests updated for the new envelope and new pagination/rate-limit tests added, including a full cursor walk.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong cross-cutting commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects the existing repository pattern and test conventions, with a mechanical convention score of 0.72 that understates the new code's quality — the flagged violations are pre-existing in untouched files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, app.py classes) or appear to be false positives on conftest.py, which contains no classes or module-level constants.

compounding_issues: Manual id assignment via SELECT MAX(id)+1 (chosen in Session 1 per the seed spec) persisted through all 5 sessions — concurrency-unsafe under parallel writes, never revisited even during the Session 4 repository refactor, and it became the load-bearing key for Session 5's cursor pagination.
The tasks table was created without AUTOINCREMENT, so later schema additions (users, email) had to be grafted on with ad-hoc PRAGMA table_info migrations rather than a uniform migration strategy.
datetime.utcnow() (deprecated in 3.12) was written in Session 1 and carried unchanged through every session's model/repository code.
Session 4's BaseRepository shipped unused generic CRUD (find_all/insert/update/delete) alongside the specialized per-owner methods — dead surface that later sessions left in place.

Session 2 briefly broke the existing suite when adding auth (16 of 28 failing mid-session) before recovering — acceptable churn, but it flagged that feature work was landed in a single large commit rather than incrementally.
key_decisions: Session 1: Kept the spec's manual id assignment (MAX(id)+1) and corrected the seed's hardcoded 'done'-vs-'pending' INSERT bug rather than blindly preserving faulty baseline code.

Session 2: Introduced JWT auth with a users table and an idempotent _migrate_add_owner_id migration that preserves pre-auth tasks (owner_id NULL) — established the per-user ownership/isolation model that all later sessions respect.
Session 3: Added Celery async email notifications with a mock sender and a users.email column migration, triggered on the pending→completed transition — clean async seam and a real integration.

Session 4: Extracted a repository layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) where repositories receive the get_db callable rather than a connection, keeping all row-level SQL out of app.py while preserving behavior exactly (test count unchanged).

Session 5: Wired Flask-Limiter keyed by JWT subject (IP fallback for auth endpoints) with a dedicated test Redis (6399) via conftest.py, and implemented keyset cursor pagination on the repository layer built in Session 4.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and monotonically across all five sessions, with the test suite growing from 13 to 47 passing tests (13→28→36→36→47) and every commit landing green. Session 1 established correctness by fixing real seed bugs; Session 2 added a non-trivial feature (auth + per-user isolation) that briefly broke tests mid-session before recovering; Session 3 integrated an external system (Celery notifications) cleanly; Session 4 was a behavior-preserving structural refactor (repository extraction, no test growth) that paid off immediately; Session 5 layered cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, pagination) on top of that clean seam. The agent consistently reasoned about the codebase rather than blindly patching — questioning spec inaccuracies in Session 1, checking test coupling before refactoring in Session 4 — and each session both preserved and extended prior behavior.
story_review.summary: A textbook five-stage arc (fix → feature → integrate → refactor → harden) with a clean repository seam enabling Session 5's cross-cutting work, marred only by the persistent manual-id concurrency decision and a few accumulated code-quality debts.
